pos: proper noun (a national god of the Philistines)
etymology: Hebrew Dagon, most likely from dagan, grain (H1715), pointing to an original character as a god of agriculture and the harvest among the Canaanite and Philistine peoples; later Jewish tradition also connected the name to dag, fish (H1709), on the strength of the ruin left of him in 1 Samuel 5:4.
biblical_def: Dagon was the national god of the Philistines, with temples at Ashdod and Gaza. When the Philistines captured the ark of God in battle, they carried it in triumph into the house of Dagon at Ashdod and set it beside him, as though the LORD were merely one captive god placed alongside another. The LORD answered the insult directly: on the first morning Dagon was found fallen on his face to the ground before the ark; set upright again, he was found the second morning fallen once more, this time with his head and both palms broken off, only the stump of him left. So notorious was the ruin that the Philistines’ own priests refused ever after to tread on the threshold of Dagon’s house at Ashdod (1Sa 5:5). Later, after Saul’s death on Gilboa, the Philistines fastened his head in the temple of Dagon and hung his armor in the house of their gods (1Ch 10:10); earlier still, Samson had been brought out to entertain the Philistine lords at a great sacrifice to Dagon, and pulled the temple down upon them in his death (Jdg 16:23-30). Every appearance of Dagon in Scripture ends the same way: a carved thing that cannot stand upright before the ark of the living God, and cannot save the men who trust it.
webster_summary: The chief idol-god of the Philistines, worshipped at Ashdod and Gaza, twice cast down before the ark of the LORD.
webster_full: DAGON, n. The national idol-god of the Philistines, worshipped at Ashdod, Gaza, and elsewhere.
His temple at Ashdod received the captured ark of the LORD, set beside him as a captive trophy.
The image was found fallen before the ark, and afterward fallen a second time with head and hands broken off.
His priests thereafter would not tread on the threshold of his house.
Saul’s head was later fastened in Dagon’s temple after the defeat at Gilboa.
scriptures: Then the lords of the Philistines gathered them together for to offer a great sacrifice unto Dagon their god, and to rejoice: for they said, Our god hath delivered Samson our enemy into our hand.
When the Philistines took the ark of God, they brought it into the house of Dagon, and set it by Dagon.
Therefore neither the priests of Dagon, nor any that come into Dagon's house, tread on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod unto this day.
And they put his armour in the house of their gods, and fastened his head in the temple of Dagon.
corruption_summary: No one burns incense to a literal fish-idol named Dagon today, so the word reads as pure antiquity; the principle it fixes — that whatever is enthroned beside the ark will not stand — is not antique at all.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nothing in the modern world worships Dagon by name, and the word carries none of the live theological battle that surrounds terms like grace or justice.

The principle to recover is what the two mornings in Ashdod actually establish: a false god does not merely fail to help; set beside the true and living God, it is broken. The Philistines meant the ark’s placement in Dagon’s house as a trophy of their god’s supremacy, and the LORD answered not with argument but with a wrecked statue on its own threshold. Every generation builds its own house of Dagon — some ultimate thing, project, or ideology set up as the thing that finally secures a people’s life and future — and every generation is offered the same lesson the Ashdodites received twice: what is not the LORD, set beside the LORD, will be found face down.
roots_summary: Hebrew dagan (H1715), grain, the likely root of Dagon’s name and character as a harvest-god of the Philistines; later folk tradition read it instead by dag, fish.
roots_lines: Hebrew dagan (H1715) — corn, grain; the probable root, marking Dagon as an agricultural, harvest deity.
Hebrew dag (H1709) — fish; a later folk-etymology suggested by the “stump” left of the idol in 1 Samuel 5:4.
Hebrew beyth Dagon — house of Dagon, the temple name at Ashdod, distinct from the place-name Beth-dagon elsewhere in Judah and Asher.
Hebrew aron (H727) — the ark, the object set beside Dagon and the instrument of his ruin.
Hebrew miphtan (H4670) — threshold; the very spot on which Dagon’s head and hands were found, and which his priests would not afterward tread.
usage: “Dagon was fallen upon his face to the ground before the ark of the LORD” — the first morning in Ashdod.
“The priests of Dagon... tread not on the threshold” — the custom his ruin produced.
“They... fastened his head in the temple of Dagon” — the same house, a different captive, after Gilboa.

pos: proper noun (the Aramaic name Christ gave to Simon Peter)
etymology: Aramaic Kepha, a rock or stone; transliterated into Greek as Kephas and rendered by its Greek translation Petros, the name by which the apostle is more commonly known in the English New Testament, Peter.
biblical_def: When Andrew first brought his brother Simon to Jesus, the Lord looked upon him and renamed him on the spot: Thou art Simon the son of Jona: thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone (Joh 1:42). The name was no passing nickname. Paul uses it repeatedly as Peter’s standing apostolic title, especially among the Jewish and Judean believers: the Corinthians divided themselves into parties, one of them naming itself after Cephas (1Co 1:12; 3:22); Paul lists Cephas among those to whom the risen Christ appeared (1Co 15:5) and among the apostles who extended him the right hand of fellowship at Jerusalem — James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars (Gal 2:9). The renaming belongs to a pattern Scripture uses elsewhere at moments of covenant significance — Abram to Abraham, Jacob to Israel — where a new name marks a new office or calling given by God’s own authority, not earned or chosen by the man himself. Cephas is therefore not merely Peter’s alternate name; it is Christ’s own naming of the man who would first confess Him as the Christ, the Son of the living God (Mat 16:16), and whom He would build His church upon in that confession.
webster_summary: The Aramaic name, meaning a rock or stone, given by Christ to Simon Peter, translated into Greek as Petros.
webster_full: CEPHAS, n. An Aramaic proper name, signifying a rock or stone.
Given by Christ to Simon at their first meeting (John 1:42).
Rendered into Greek as Petros, whence the English Peter.
Used by Paul as Peter’s standing apostolic title among the Jerusalem church.
One of the pillars named alongside James and John (Galatians 2:9).
scriptures: Joh 1:42
And he brought him to Jesus. And when Jesus beheld him, he said, Thou art Simon the son of Jona: thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone.
Now this I say, that every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ.
Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours;
Gal 2:9

And when James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given unto me, they gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship; that we should go unto the heathen, and they unto the circumcision.
corruption_summary: Rome builds the entire structure of papal primacy on this renaming, reading Christ’s words to Peter as investing him and his supposed successors with perpetual, supreme, transferable authority over the whole church; the text will not bear that weight.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the doctrine of Petrine primacy that grew into the papacy: the claim that Christ’s naming of Simon as Cephas, and the later word thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church (Mat 16:18), installed Peter as the first pope, holding a supreme, monarchical authority over the universal church, transmissible in perpetuity to the bishops of Rome as his successors. This reading treats a personal name and a single confessional moment as a constitutional charter for an entire ecclesial office never described anywhere else in the New Testament.

The Reformed reading takes the text as it stands: the rock in Matthew 16:18 follows directly from Peter’s own confession the verse before — Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God (Mat 16:16) — so that it is the confessed truth, Christ’s own identity, that is the church’s foundation, with Peter honored as the first to speak it plainly. That Cephas was no infallible monarch over his brother apostles is settled by Paul’s own testimony: when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed (Gal 2:11). An apostle rebuked to his face for a real fault is not the model of a supreme, error-proof office; he is one pillar among others, honored by name, but answerable to the same gospel he was given to preach.
roots_summary: Aramaic kepha, a rock, given by Christ as Simon’s new name and carried into Greek as Petros, the source of the English Peter.
roots_lines: Aramaic kepha — a rock or stone, the underlying word behind Cephas.
Greek Kephas — the direct transliteration of the Aramaic, used by Paul as a proper name.
Greek petros — a stone, the Greek translation of Cephas, whence the English Peter.
Greek petra — a mass of rock, bedrock; the word Christ uses for the foundation in Matthew 16:18, distinguished by some Reformed exegetes from petros.
Hebrew precedent — the pattern of a divinely given new name marking a new office, as with Abram to Abraham and Jacob to Israel.
usage: “Thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone” — Christ’s own naming of Simon.
“James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars” — his standing among the apostles at Jerusalem.
“I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed” — Paul’s rebuke, against any claim of Cephas’s supremacy.

pos: proper noun (a king of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat)
etymology: Hebrew Yehoram, “the LORD is exalted,” from Yeho-, a shortened form of the covenant name, and ram, high or exalted. Not to be confused with his brother-in-law and contemporary Joram, king of Israel and son of Ahab (see the separate entry).
biblical_def: Jehoram was the son of the godly Jehoshaphat and became king of Judah in his father’s stead, but he did not walk in his father’s way. He had married Athaliah, the daughter of Ahab, and through that marriage he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as did the house of Ahab (2Ki 8:18). His first recorded act as king was to secure his throne by murder: he rose up to the kingdom of his father, strengthened himself, and slew all his brethren with the sword, and divers also of the princes of Israel (2Ch 21:4). His reign of eight years brought Edom and Libnah into revolt, and Elijah sent him a written prophecy of disease and disaster for having made Judah to go a whoring, and forcing Judah thereto. That judgment fell exactly: he died of an incurable bowel disease, and his people made no burning for him, like the burning of his fathers. He departed without being desired, and though buried in the city of David, it was not in the sepulchres of the kings (2Ch 21:20). Scripture makes his contrast with his father explicit and deliberate: a covenant heir, married into an idolatrous house, undoing in one generation what a godly father had labored to build.
webster_summary: A king of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat, who married Athaliah of the house of Ahab and led Judah into apostasy; died unlamented and unburied among the kings.
webster_full: JEHORAM, n. A king of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat and husband of Athaliah, daughter of Ahab.
He murdered his brothers to secure his throne upon his accession.
He walked in the way of the kings of Israel through his marriage into Ahab’s house.
He received written judgment from Elijah and died of a grievous disease.
He was buried in the city of David, but not among the sepulchres of the kings.
scriptures: And in the fifth year of Joram the son of Ahab king of Israel, Jehoshaphat being then king of Judah, Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah began to reign.
And he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as did the house of Ahab: for the daughter of Ahab was his wife: and he did evil in the sight of the LORD.
Now when Jehoram was risen up to the kingdom of his father, he strengthened himself, and slew all his brethren with the sword, and divers also of the princes of Israel.

Thirty and two years old was he when he began to reign, and he reigned in Jerusalem eight years, and departed without being desired. Howbeit they buried him in the city of David, but not in the sepulchres of the kings.
corruption_summary: No modern movement has redefined Jehoram; the principle his life fixes — that marriage into an ungodly house can undo a generation of covenant faithfulness — is simply ignored rather than argued against.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Jehoram is not a contested figure; he is a largely forgotten one, which is its own kind of loss, since the pattern his reign fixes is exactly the pattern many households still walk into with open eyes.

The principle to recover is the force of 2 Chronicles 21’s own verdict: he was Jehoshaphat’s son, raised under a reforming, covenant-keeping king, yet the daughter of Ahab was his wife, and by that single alliance the way of the kings of Israel entered Judah’s throne. Scripture does not blame Jehoram’s apostasy on ignorance or on distant ancestry; it names the marriage as the hinge. A household’s covenant faithfulness is not self-perpetuating by pedigree alone; it is a trust that can be undone within a single generation by exactly the alliance Jehoram made, and the text’s closing detail — buried, but not among the kings, departed without being desired — is Scripture’s own judgment on where that road ends.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yehoram, “the LORD is exalted,” a name shared with his Israelite counterpart Joram, whom Scripture and later usage distinguish by the fuller form Jehoram for the king of Judah.
roots_lines: Hebrew Yeho- — a shortened form of the covenant name YHWH, prefixed to many royal Judahite names.
Hebrew ram — high, exalted, lifted up; the root shared with words for height and pride.
2 Kings 8:16 names him son of Jehoshaphat, distinguishing him at once from Joram son of Ahab in the same verse.
2 Chronicles 21 supplies the fullest and most severe account of his reign, including Elijah’s written prophecy against him.
His marriage to Athaliah later brought the house of David to the brink of extinction under her own usurpation (2 Kings 11).
usage: “He walked in the way of the kings of Israel... for the daughter of Ahab was his wife” — the hinge of his apostasy.
“He strengthened himself, and slew all his brethren with the sword” — his first act as king.
“He departed without being desired” — Scripture’s verdict on his death.

pos: proper noun (a prophet in the days of Jehoiakim, son of Shemaiah)
etymology: Hebrew Uriyyah, “the LORD is my light,” the identical name and meaning borne generations earlier by Uriah the Hittite, husband of Bathsheba (see the separate entry); a different man, of a different family, in a different century.
biblical_def: Urijah the son of Shemaiah of Kirjathjearim prophesied in the name of the LORD in the days of King Jehoiakim, and his message was the same as Jeremiah’s own: he prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah (Jer 26:20). Where Jehoiakim heard Jeremiah’s preaching with fury, he answered Urijah’s identical message by seeking to put him to death. Urijah fled in fear to Egypt, but the king sent men after him, fetched him out of Egypt, and brought him before Jehoiakim, who slew him with the sword, and cast his dead body into the graves of the common people (Jer 26:23) — denied even an honorable burial. The account is preserved inside the larger narrative of Jeremiah’s own trial for the very same preaching (Jer 26), where certain princes and elders intervened and Jeremiah’s life was spared. Urijah’s martyrdom stands beside Jeremiah’s deliverance as two outcomes of one faithfulness, both entirely in the hand of the LORD’s providence rather than the courage or caution of the men themselves.
webster_summary: A prophet under King Jehoiakim who preached the same message as Jeremiah, fled to Egypt in fear of the king, and was extradited and put to death.
webster_full: URIJAH, n. A prophet of the LORD in the reign of Jehoiakim, son of Shemaiah of Kirjathjearim.
He prophesied against Jerusalem and Judah in words identical to Jeremiah’s.
Jehoiakim sought his life for this preaching.
He fled to Egypt, but was fetched back and delivered to the king.
He was put to death and denied burial among honored men.
scriptures: And there was also a man that prophesied in the name of the LORD, Urijah the son of Shemaiah of Kirjathjearim, who prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah:

And when Jehoiakim the king, with all his mighty men, and all the princes, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death: but when Urijah heard it, he was afraid, and fled, and went into Egypt;
And Jehoiakim the king sent men into Egypt, namely, Elnathan the son of Achbor, and certain men with him into Egypt.
And they fetched forth Urijah out of Egypt, and brought him unto Jehoiakim the king; who slew him with the sword, and cast his dead body into the graves of the common people.
corruption_summary: No modern reinterpretation targets Urijah; the corruption to name is the standing temptation to treat a lesser-known martyr’s fate as evidence against the faithfulness of the message he shared with a better-known prophet.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Urijah is obscure precisely because his story survives only inside Jeremiah’s own trial narrative, a single paragraph naming a man history otherwise forgot.

The principle to recover is what that single paragraph is doing inside Jeremiah 26 at all: it is not a digression but the point. Jeremiah stood trial for the same words Urijah preached, and one prophet was delivered while the other was killed. Scripture does not explain the difference by Jeremiah’s greater faith or Urijah’s lesser courage — Urijah, after all, prophesied publicly before he fled, and his fear came only after the king’s wrath was declared. The outcome rested in the hand of the LORD working through the princes who intervened for Jeremiah, not in the character of the messengers. A true word from the LORD is not vindicated by the messenger’s survival, nor is a faithful messenger condemned by his death; both men spoke the same word, and the LORD disposed of each life according to His own counsel.
roots_summary: Hebrew Uriyyah, “the LORD is my light,” a name Scripture gives to more than one man, distinguished here by patronym and by the era of Jehoiakim rather than David.
roots_lines: Hebrew uri — my light, from or, light.
Hebrew Yah — the shortened covenant name, appended as the theophoric element.
Son of Shemaiah, of Kirjathjearim — the patronym and hometown Jeremiah 26 supplies to distinguish him.
Contemporary of Jeremiah, under King Jehoiakim, roughly a century after Uriah the Hittite’s death under David.
His account is preserved only within Jeremiah 26, the record of Jeremiah’s own trial for the identical message.
usage: “Who prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah” — his message, identical to Jeremiah’s.
“He was afraid, and fled, and went into Egypt” — his flight from Jehoiakim’s wrath.
“Slew him with the sword, and cast his dead body into the graves of the common people” — his martyrdom.

pos: proper noun, plural (the local Baal-idols of Canaan)
etymology: Hebrew plural of Baal, “lord” or “master” (H1168), formed with the masculine plural suffix -im. The plural denotes not one deity worshipped under many titles but the many local, territorial Baal-cults scattered across Canaan, each attached to a particular hill, town, or shrine.
biblical_def: Baalim is the standing plural Scripture reaches for whenever it names Israel’s besetting, generational idolatry rather than a single act of it. The book of Judges opens its whole downward cycle with the formula: the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the LORD, and served Baalim (Jdg 2:11), repeated almost verbatim at 3:7 with the added note that they forgat the LORD their God. The plural matters: this was not devotion transferred wholesale to one rival god but a scattering of allegiance across many local lords, each shrine offering its own claim on a harvest or a household, so that the nation’s worship fragmented even as it apostatized. The same plural returns at the hinge-points of repentance: Samuel calls Israel to put away the Baalim and Ashtaroth, and serve the LORD only (1Sa 7:4), and Israel’s own confession before Samuel names the same sin: we have forsaken the LORD, and have served Baalim and Ashtaroth (1Sa 12:10). Baalim is therefore Scripture’s word for idolatry in its ordinary, un-dramatic form: not one great apostasy but many small, local, competing loyalties, each easier to excuse than a single rival god would be, and each requiring the same putting-away before true repentance can begin.
webster_summary: The plural of Baal; the many local Baal-idols of Canaan collectively, served by Israel in the recurring apostasy of the Judges period.
webster_full: BAALIM, n. pl. The Baal-idols of Canaan, considered collectively; plural of Baal.
Named repeatedly in Judges as the object of Israel’s recurring national apostasy.
Often paired with Ashtaroth, the corresponding female Canaanite deities.
Put away at Samuel’s call as a condition of Israel’s deliverance from the Philistines.
Named in Israel’s own later confession of national sin under Samuel.
scriptures: Jdg 2:11
And the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the LORD, and served Baalim:
Jdg 3:7
And the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the LORD, and forgat the LORD their God, and served Baalim and the groves.
Then the children of Israel did put away Baalim and Ashtaroth, and served the LORD only.

And they cried unto the LORD, and said, We have sinned, because we have forsaken the LORD, and have served Baalim and Ashtaroth: but now deliver us out of the hand of our enemies, and we will serve thee.
corruption_summary: No one today argues for Baal-worship by name; the corruption is imagining that idolatry must look like a single dramatic rival religion rather than the scattered, local, easily-excused loyalties the plural Baalim actually names.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nobody defends Baalim as a live religious option, and the word itself carries no contested modern meaning.

The principle to recover is exactly what the plural form preserves and a singular Baal would obscure: idolatry in Judges is not primarily one great national apostasy to a single named rival but a scattering of loyalty across many small, local claims, each more plausible on its own than open rebellion against the LORD would be. A single town’s shrine, a single household’s harvest-god, a single field’s local lord — none of these announced itself as treason against the covenant, which is precisely how the cycle in Judges kept renewing itself generation after generation. Samuel’s call to put away the Baalim and Ashtaroth, and serve the LORD only names the actual shape repentance takes: not the rejection of one obvious rival, but the systematic putting-away of every scattered, half-acknowledged, locally-tolerated claim on an allegiance that belongs to the LORD alone.
roots_summary: Hebrew plural of Baal (H1168), lord or master, denoting the many local Canaanite Baal-cults rather than one deity under one name.
roots_lines: Hebrew Baal (H1168) — lord, master, possessor, owner; the singular root.
Hebrew -im — the ordinary masculine plural suffix, here marking true multiplicity of local cults rather than a plural of majesty.
Frequently paired with Ashtaroth (H6252), the plural of the corresponding Canaanite goddess Ashtoreth.
The formula “did evil in the sight of the LORD, and served Baalim” recurs as the standing refrain opening each cycle in Judges.
Put away at Samuel’s command in 1 Samuel 7:4 as the necessary first act before Israel’s deliverance from the Philistines.
usage: “The children of Israel did evil in the sight of the LORD, and served Baalim” — the standing refrain of Judges.
“Put away Baalim and Ashtaroth, and served the LORD only” — the shape of true repentance.
“We have forsaken the LORD, and have served Baalim and Ashtaroth” — Israel’s own confession.

pos: proper noun (the derisive name Hezekiah gave the brazen serpent when he destroyed it as an idol)
etymology: Hebrew Nechushtan, from nechosheth (H5178), bronze or brass, formed with a diminishing and contemptuous force — something close to “a mere piece of brass.” The name itself was Hezekiah’s own coinage at the moment of destruction, chosen precisely to strip the object of a reverence it had wrongly accumulated.
biblical_def: The object Hezekiah named Nehushtan began centuries earlier as an act of God’s own commanded mercy. When fiery serpents afflicted Israel in the wilderness for their sin, the LORD told Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live (Num 21:8). Moses made a serpent of brass, and whoever looked upon it in faith after being bitten lived (Num 21:9). Christ Himself later took this exact event as a type of His own crucifixion: as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up (Joh 3:14). But the preserved bronze object outlived its moment. By Hezekiah’s reign, centuries later, Judah had begun burning incense to it as though the relic itself, rather than the LORD who had commanded its making, held saving power. Hezekiah’s reforms removed the high places, brake the images, cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made... and he called it Nehushtan (2Ki 18:4) — a mere brazen thing, unworthy of the incense the people had given it. A means of grace, kept past its appointed use and venerated for itself, had become an idol; the king who honored the LORD destroyed it for that very reason.
webster_summary: The bronze serpent Moses made at God’s command in the wilderness, later worshipped as an idol and destroyed by King Hezekiah, who gave it the contemptuous name Nehushtan.
webster_full: NEHUSHTAN, n. The derisive name given by King Hezekiah to the bronze serpent of Moses when he destroyed it as an object of idolatrous worship.
The serpent itself was made by Moses at God’s command in the wilderness (Numbers 21).
Whoever looked upon it in faith after being bitten by a fiery serpent lived.
Centuries later Judah burned incense to the preserved relic as an idol.
Hezekiah broke it in pieces in his reforms and named it Nehushtan, a mere thing of brass.
scriptures: He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan.
Num 21:8
And the LORD said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.
Num 21:9
And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.
Joh 3:14
And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up:
corruption_summary: The modern instinct is to assume idolatry always begins with something false; Nehushtan shows it can begin with something God Himself commanded, kept past its purpose and venerated for itself instead of for what it typified.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. No one today argues for bowing before bronze serpents, and the word itself is rare even among the doctrinally literate.

The principle to recover is the uncomfortable one Hezekiah’s reform insists on: this was not a foreign idol smuggled in from Canaan but a God-ordained object of His own commanded mercy, and it became an idol anyway, by nothing more than being kept and reverenced past its appointed use. Every means of grace carries this same danger — a sacrament, a hymn, a translation, a preacher, a revival, a church building, even a right doctrine rightly formulated — can be so venerated for itself that it eclipses the LORD it was given to point toward. Hezekiah is commended in Scripture precisely for being willing to break what his own fathers had kept sacred, once it had ceased to serve its purpose and become the object of worship in its own right. The serpent that once meant look and live had become a thing the nation looked at instead of the LORD; Hezekiah’s name for it, a mere piece of brass, is the corrective every generation needs applied to whatever its own Nehushtan has become.
roots_summary: Hebrew Nechushtan, from nechosheth, bronze or brass (H5178), a contemptuous coinage by Hezekiah stripping the once-venerated relic of its wrongly accumulated reverence.
roots_lines: Hebrew nechosheth (H5178) — bronze, brass, copper; the base noun.
The -an ending gives the word a diminishing, almost mocking force: a mere brazen thing.
Hebrew nachash (H5175) — serpent; the word for the object itself in Numbers 21, distinct from but audibly close to Nehushtan.
The object’s original purpose: whoever looked upon it in faith after being bitten lived (Numbers 21:8-9).
Christ’s own use of the type in John 3:14 fixes its true and lasting meaning, in contrast to Judah’s later idolatrous use of the relic itself.
usage: “He brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made... and he called it Nehushtan” — Hezekiah’s reform.
“Every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live” — its original, God-commanded purpose.
“As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up” — Christ’s own use of the type.

etymology: Named for Moses Amyraut (1596-1664), a French Huguenot theologian of the Academy of Saumur, who taught a modified doctrine of the extent of the atonement sometimes called hypothetical universalism or the Saumur hypothesis, and more commonly Amyraldism or Amyraldianism.
biblical_def: Amyraldianism reorders the logical sequence of God’s eternal decrees regarding salvation. On the Amyraldian scheme, God first (in the order of logic, not of time) decrees to send Christ to die for all men without exception, conditioned on their faith — the atonement made universally sufficient and, in that sense, universally intended. Then, seeing by His foreknowledge that no fallen sinner would believe of his own will, God decrees a second, particular election, choosing some to whom He grants the effectual gift of faith. The system was devised to hold together universal-sounding texts (such as God’s desire that all men be saved) with the particular texts of election, without simply reading the universal texts as addressed to all kinds of men rather than every individual man, as the historic Reformed reading does. The doctrine was controversial within Reformed orthodoxy from its first appearance; the Formula Consensus Helvetica (1675) was drafted substantially to require subscription against it in the Swiss Reformed churches, on the ground that it introduces an unnecessary and unscriptural universal intention into the eternal decree, and risks becoming, in less careful hands, a halfway house toward a fuller Arminian scheme in which the human will, not God’s sovereign election, becomes the final deciding factor in who is actually saved.
webster_summary: The theological system of Moses Amyraut, positing a universal but conditional divine intention in the atonement, followed by a particular election of those granted faith; rejected by the Reformed orthodox as compromising the doctrine of particular redemption.
webster_full: AMYRALDIANISM, n. (soteriology / historical theology) The system of Moses Amyraut (1596-1664) of the Academy of Saumur.
Also called hypothetical universalism or the Saumur hypothesis.
Posits a logically prior universal, conditional divine intention in Christ’s death.
Followed by a particular election of those to whom saving faith is actually granted.
Answered by the Formula Consensus Helvetica (1675), which required subscription against it.
scriptures: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep.
Eph 5:25
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;
Mat 1:21
And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.
corruption_summary: Amyraldianism softens particular redemption by inserting a logically prior universal intention into the atonement that Scripture does not require, and that the specific objects of Christ’s death named throughout the New Testament — His sheep, His church, His people — do not support.
corruption_paragraphs: Amyraldianism is the system that inserts, logically prior to God’s particular election, a universal and merely conditional divine intention in the atonement: Christ is said to have died for all men in a sense that secures nothing for anyone apart from a further, separately decreed gift of faith to the elect alone. The doctrine is a genuine attempt at reverence toward the whole counsel of Scripture, not a careless error, which is exactly why the Reformed churches judged it necessary to answer it formally rather than ignore it.

The Reformed answer is drawn from how Scripture itself describes the object of Christ’s death: not an undifferentiated mass of humanity but a specific, named people. The good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep, not for the whole flock of the world indiscriminately (Joh 10:11, 15); Christ loved the church, and gave himself for it, a particular bride, not humanity in general (Eph 5:25); and He is named Jesus for this very reason, that he shall save his people from their sins — not merely make salvation possible for anyone who might believe, but actually save those given to Him (Mat 1:21). Particular redemption holds that Christ’s death actually and efficaciously secures the salvation of the elect, accomplishing precisely what it intends, rather than merely making salvation possible pending a further condition. The Amyraldian scheme, however carefully qualified, still locates the final decisive factor in whether a given sinner is granted faith, a second decree standing behind the first; the Reformed doctrine holds that election and redemption were never two decrees but one single, sovereign purpose, accomplishing from eternity exactly what it secures in time.
roots_summary: Named for Moses Amyraut of the Academy of Saumur, whose hypothetical-universalist scheme was formally answered by the Formula Consensus Helvetica of 1675.
roots_lines: Moses Amyraut (1596-1664) — French Huguenot theologian of the Academy of Saumur, the doctrine’s namesake.
Also called hypothetical universalism, naming the conditional, non-securing character of the universal intention.
Also called the Saumur hypothesis, after the French academy where it was taught.
Formula Consensus Helvetica (1675) — the Swiss Reformed confessional document drafted substantially to answer it.
Contrasted throughout Reformed orthodoxy with particular redemption, the doctrine that Christ’s death actually secures the salvation of the elect alone.
usage: Amyraldianism: the system of a logically prior universal, conditional atonement followed by particular election.
Answered by the Formula Consensus Helvetica (1675) as a departure from particular redemption.
Contrasted with the Reformed doctrine that Christ’s death actually and efficaciously secures the salvation of the elect.

etymology: Greek arche, first, beginning, original, and typos, pattern, stamp, impression; Latin theologia archetypa, a term of Reformed and Lutheran scholastic prolegomena distinguishing God’s own self-knowledge from the derivative knowledge He grants to creatures (see the companion entry, Ectypal Theology).
biblical_def: Archetypal theology is the technical name Reformed orthodox theologians of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries gave to God’s own perfect, infinite, and incommunicable knowledge of Himself. It is not a body of doctrine that any creature, however exalted, could come to hold; it simply is God, identical with His own infinite self-understanding, wholly beyond the reach of any finite mind. Scripture presses this point repeatedly: Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection? (Job 11:7); the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God (1Co 2:11); how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! (Rom 11:33). The distinction between archetypal and ectypal theology guards two truths at once. First, that theology given to creatures (ectypal theology) is genuinely true and not illusory, since it is a real communication from God rather than mere human guesswork. Second, that no creature ever comes to possess God’s own infinite self-knowledge; the gap between archetype and ectype is not a matter of degree that more revelation, more study, or even final glorification could close, but a difference of nature between the Creator’s own self-knowing and any creature’s reception of what He discloses. This distinction is the foundation of a properly humble theological method: even the truest theology done by regenerate men remains a finite echo of the original, never a possession of it.
webster_summary: In Reformed scholastic theology, God’s own perfect and infinite self-knowledge, identical with God Himself and incommunicable to any creature, distinguished from the finite ectypal theology given by revelation.
webster_full: ARCHETYPAL THEOLOGY, n. (theological prolegomena) God’s own infinite, perfect self-knowledge.
Not a body of doctrine creatures can hold, but identical with God’s own being.
Distinguished from ectypal theology, the finite, derivative knowledge given to creatures.
Developed by the Reformed orthodox of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries (e.g., Junius).
Grounds a properly humble theological method: even true creaturely theology remains a finite echo, not a possession, of the original.
scriptures: For what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him? even so the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God.
Job 11:7
Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?
O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!
Who hath directed the Spirit of the LORD, or being his counsellor hath taught him?
corruption_summary: A scholastic term with no direct modern cultural target, but its abandonment is exactly what underwrites the rationalist confidence that the human mind can, in principle, attain exhaustive knowledge of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Archetypal theology is not a contested word in the wider culture; it is largely forgotten, which is itself the loss worth naming.

The principle to recover is the corrective this distinction was built to supply against post-Enlightenment rationalist theology, which in its confidence that reason unaided could systematize the whole of God quietly assumed there was no real difference in kind between God’s own self-knowledge and the theology a sufficiently rigorous mind could construct — only a difference of degree, closable by better method or more information. Deuteronomy 29:29 fixes the actual boundary: the secret things belong unto the LORD our God, and only those things which are revealed belong unto us. Archetypal theology names what remains forever on the far side of that line; it is the reason theology, at its healthiest, ends every chapter in worship rather than mastery, and why Job’s question — canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection? — is not answered yes by any degree of human learning, only by the God who condescends to be known in the manner ectypal theology describes.
roots_summary: Greek arche (first, original) and typos (pattern), Latin theologia archetypa, a Reformed scholastic term for God’s own incommunicable self-knowledge.
roots_lines: Greek arche — beginning, origin, first principle.
Greek typos — a pattern, stamp, or impression from which a copy is made.
Latin theologia archetypa — the scholastic technical term, coined especially by the Reformed theologian Franciscus Junius (1545-1602).
Paired throughout Reformed prolegomena with theologia ectypa, ectypal theology, the revealed copy given to creatures.
Distinct from mere divine incomprehensibility as a vague sentiment; the term names a precise, structured distinction in theological method.
usage: Archetypal theology: God’s own infinite self-knowledge, identical with His being.
Distinguished from ectypal theology, the finite copy given to creatures by revelation.
“How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out” — the boundary the term marks.

etymology: Greek ek, out of, from, and typos, pattern, stamp, impression; Latin theologia ectypa, the finite copy or impression of the divine archetype, given to creatures in a manner accommodated to their capacity (see the companion entry, Archetypal Theology).
biblical_def: Ectypal theology is the Reformed scholastic term for the true but finite, derivative, and accommodated knowledge of God that He grants to creatures, in contrast to His own infinite archetypal self-knowledge. The Reformed orthodox distinguished several kinds of ectypal theology by the capacity of the recipient: the theology of union, the human knowledge possessed by Christ’s own human nature; the theology of vision, the fuller knowledge granted to glorified saints and angels who behold God face to face; and the theology of pilgrims (theologia viatorum), the theology of Scripture given to believers still on earth, our present possession. Scripture describes this last kind directly: God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets (Heb 1:1) — a real but staged and accommodated communication, suited to what the hearers could receive. Even the fullest ectypal theology available to any creature remains ectypal rather than archetypal: For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD (Isa 55:8), and even glorified knowledge does not close the gap in kind: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known (1Co 13:12) — a promise of far fuller, unmediated knowledge, yet still creaturely, still received rather than possessed as God possesses His own.
webster_summary: In Reformed scholastic theology, the finite, derivative, accommodated knowledge of God given to creatures by revelation, distinguished from God’s own infinite archetypal self-knowledge.
webster_full: ECTYPAL THEOLOGY, n. (theological prolegomena) The finite, derivative theology given to creatures by God’s revelation.
Distinguished from archetypal theology, God’s own infinite, incommunicable self-knowledge.
Subdivided by Reformed scholastics into the theology of union, of vision, and of pilgrims (theologia viatorum).
The theology of pilgrims is the theology of Scripture, given to believers still on earth.
Even the fullest creaturely knowledge of God, in glory, remains ectypal rather than archetypal.
scriptures: The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.
Isa 55:8
For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD.
Heb 1:1
God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets,
For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
corruption_summary: A scholastic term with no live cultural target, but the principle it protects — that revealed theology, though real and true, is always accommodated and never exhaustive — is exactly what is lost when Scripture is treated as either a bare human record or a complete metaphysical system.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Ectypal theology is a technical term of historical prolegomena, not a word under present cultural dispute.

The principle to recover runs in two directions at once, and both are needed. Against liberal and historical-critical instincts that treat revelation as merely human religious reflection dressed up in divine language, ectypal theology insists the revealed word is genuinely God’s own communication, true as far as it goes, not myth or projection: those things which are revealed belong unto us (Deu 29:29). Against the opposite rationalist instinct, which treats systematic theology as though it could, given enough precision, close every gap and answer every question about God’s own inner life, ectypal theology insists the revealed word remains an accommodation — for my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways (Isa 55:8) — suited to creaturely capacity rather than a transcript of the archetype. Even Paul, writing under inspiration, describes his own knowledge as now... in part (1Co 13:12); the theologian’s task is neither to doubt the truth of what is given nor to mistake it for the whole of what could be known, but to receive the ectype gratefully as the LORD’s own gracious accommodation to those who could bear no more.
roots_summary: Greek ek (from, out of) and typos (pattern), Latin theologia ectypa, the Reformed scholastic term for revealed, creaturely theology, subdivided into union, vision, and pilgrim theology.
roots_lines: Greek ek — out of, from, marking derivation from the archetype.
Greek typos — a pattern, stamp, or impression; the same root shared with archetypal theology.
Theologia unionis — the theology of union, Christ’s own human knowledge of God.
Theologia visionis — the theology of vision, possessed by glorified saints and angels.
Theologia viatorum — the theology of pilgrims, the theology of Scripture given to believers on earth.
usage: Ectypal theology: the finite, revealed copy of God’s own archetypal self-knowledge.
Subdivided into the theology of union, of vision, and of pilgrims (theologia viatorum).
“Now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known” — ectypal knowledge, even in glory.

pos: noun (Christology; patristic and Reformed scholastic term)
etymology: Greek an-, without, and hypostasis, subsistence, person; a negative Christological term stating that the human nature Christ assumed has no independent personal subsistence of its own, apart from union with the eternal Person of the divine Word.
biblical_def: Anhypostasis is the doctrine that in the incarnation, the human nature Christ took to Himself — a true body and a reasonable soul — never existed, and never exists, as its own separate human person. It has no independent who apart from the eternal Person (hypostasis) of the divine Word, who alone is the personal subject of the incarnate Christ. The doctrine safeguards against Nestorianism, the ancient error of dividing Christ into two persons, a human person joined alongside the divine, as though the man Jesus were someone in addition to the Son of God rather than the Son of God become man. The positive corollary, enhypostasis, states what anhypostasis alone might seem to deny: the human nature, precisely because it has no person of its own, is not left personless in any defective sense, but has its personal reality by, in, and through its union with the divine Word who assumes it. Together the two terms preserve the single-subject Christology confessed at Chalcedon (451): one Person, two natures, unconfused, unchanged, undivided, unseparated. John 1:14 describes exactly this: the Word was made flesh — not the Word joining an already-existing human person, but the Word Himself becoming flesh, taking a human nature that has its personal reality solely in Him, made in the likeness of men (Php 2:7), partaker of flesh and blood as the children are (Heb 2:14), so that in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily (Col 2:9).
webster_summary: In Christology, the doctrine that Christ’s human nature has no independent personal subsistence apart from the divine Word, who alone is the person of the incarnate Christ; paired with the corollary doctrine of enhypostasis.
webster_full: ANHYPOSTASIS, n. (Christology) The doctrine that Christ’s human nature has no independent personhood of its own.
Guards against Nestorianism, which divides Christ into two persons.
Paired with enhypostasis: the human nature has its personal reality in union with the divine Word.
Preserves the single-subject Christology confessed at the Council of Chalcedon (451).
Grounded in John 1:14: the Word Himself made flesh, not joined to an already-existing human person.
scriptures: Joh 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
Php 2:7
But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:
Heb 2:14

Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil;
Col 2:9
For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
corruption_summary: Popular imagination often pictures the incarnation as God simply inhabiting an already-existing man named Jesus, which is functionally the ancient Nestorian error anhypostasis was formulated to exclude.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Anhypostasis is a technical patristic and scholastic term, not a word under live cultural dispute.

The principle to recover is the precision this term guards against a very natural but mistaken way of picturing the incarnation: the idea, common in loose popular devotion and in some modern kenotic Christologies, of God the Son simply indwelling or empowering an independently-existing human individual named Jesus, as though the human Jesus were someone in his own right whom the divine Word then joined. Scripture will not permit that picture. John 1:14 does not say the Word joined Himself to flesh already possessing its own personal center; it says the Word was made flesh — the Word Himself is the one acting, becoming, taking to Himself a human nature that has never for one moment existed apart from Him. This is not a technicality without consequence: if Christ’s human nature had its own independent person, the sufferings of that nature would belong to a human person distinct from the Son of God, and the atonement would lose the very thing that gives it infinite worth — that it is the eternal Son Himself, in His assumed humanity, who bled, died, and rose. Anhypostasis and its corollary enhypostasis together secure that the one who suffered and the one who saves are, without division, the same single Person.
roots_summary: Greek an- (without) and hypostasis (person, subsistence), a patristic and Reformed scholastic Christological term guarding the single personhood of Christ against Nestorianism.
roots_lines: Greek an- — a negating prefix, without or lacking.
Greek hypostasis — subsistence, underlying reality, person; the same word rendered “person” in Trinitarian and Christological formulas.
Paired with enhypostasis, the positive corollary: personhood in and through union with the Word.
Developed in patristic Christology to answer Nestorianism, the division of Christ into two persons.
Confirmed by the Council of Chalcedon (451): one Person, two natures, unconfused, unchanged, undivided, unseparated.
usage: Anhypostasis: Christ’s human nature has no independent personhood of its own.
Paired with enhypostasis: its personal reality is in and through union with the divine Word.
“The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” — the doctrine’s biblical ground.
